translations.2ce4b1a8e6869d3bb99b9398: Each agent principle has a known pair in people management, in the same order you hire, guide, hold accountable, and evaluate.
translations.85d7d0d2918c2f9d8628f5b2: ⟪P0⟫Role⟪P1⟫intention, so you know why the opening exists.
translations.19eac639eb14ddc56a08fa13: ⟪P0⟫Onboarding⟪P1⟫context, what you teach on day one.
translations.d8bd9bfbd571c34840c39343: ⟪P0⟫Level of authority⟪P1⟫autonomy, “up to R$ 500 you decide”.
translations.8094d018594e6eb86359bba0: ⟪P0⟫1⟪P1⟫1: supervision, review, correct, or decide whether to promote or not.
translations.53a1d32df60587859c4538a3: ✓ Ask “how would I do this with a new employee?” before writing any instruction.
translations.6272702a4d14f11544d1632a: ✗ Treat agent management like a technical topic that only programmers understand.
translations.50dbf3a1667ab7d7a05505a8: Take an employee or colleague you’ve already guided and list what you told them in the first week. Mark which principle each item corresponds to.
translations.5e964261eec665c932fe0dc2: Usually, you find the house rules (context), where to look for information (data), and what they can decide on their own (autonomy). What’s often missing is the written criterion, because with people it gets adjusted in conversation. With an agent, it needs to be in the role.
translations.1bdb8fdb7a22f5ea8e2a9117: What the agent doesn’t “figure out on its own”
translations.ba62c0895e03881f1ed4a208: Only the written part reaches the agent; what stayed only in your head—or is “obvious” to the team—gets lost along the way.
translations.a1e88bb3adad28e41669de38: ⟪P0⟫Tone⟪P1⟫how to speak to a client, formal or close.
translations.eda649d26aec7a1460d06d09: ⟪P0⟫Source⟪P1⟫which spreadsheet or system is valid, and which isn’t.
translations.bcf82b7fce88512cf7cb550b: ⟪P0⟫If something is missing⟪P1⟫what to do when the data doesn’t exist.
translations.74224cebe38e283e9416e244: What you know: identify the initial condition.
translations.dcd91dd01325fe0d8d7acb2e: What’s obvious: apply the described decision.
translations.9df1d2eaefb020bd71042959: What’s written: check the effect in the example.
translations.77c2437e7b64f154bba92466: What the agent uses: record the output evidence.
translations.22da7830178163ea35614aca: ✓ Write the rule “if information is missing” in every instruction, even if it seems like an exaggeration.
translations.c5dec760f31a7108b0fc84fe: ✗ Assume the agent will notice the right tone or the correct source “from context”.
translations.41ab4056d4294f7786338a85: List three things that anyone on your team knows without anyone saying them. Rewrite each one as an instruction sentence.
translations.3341c884535f391f8de28d03: Example: “nobody responds to customers after 8pm” becomes “don’t send messages after 8pm; leave them as a draft for the morning”. The exercise shows how much of the operation depends on rules that are never written down.
translations.216b93203736bc52ce4aa9a7: People who program with agents already live this.
translations.5ccab06aeb58ba328d796f7b: The flow of a code agent follows the same principles: combine, contextualize, verify, limit, and review.
translations.f4106dea6cec61fdf00a930f: ⟪P0⟫⟪P2⟫⟪P1⟫context, the house rules in a file.
translations.d7597480884c2e9d7ab400da: ✓ Copy from programming the rule “ready is what can be proven, not what is declared”.
translations.80b85ab87d219f019de124ea: ✗ Think these practices only serve people who write code.
translations.5634f92479c7509cebd12fae: Choose two items from the list (for example, planned mode and failure log) and describe how you would apply each one to a task that isn’t programming.
translations.6944ce2df51119524a914b04: Planned mode becomes “show me the email script before sending”; failure log becomes a table with date, error, and the agent’s support-team correction. The practice is the same; only the object changes.
translations.671db50641f323b323d0924f: Permission modes are the N0–N4 ladder with a button
